summary: Defines a generic YANG grouping for geographic locations. It lets YANG data models specify a position on or relative to Earth or another astronomical object, so each model need not define its own way of expressing it.

eli5.summary: A ready-made form for writing down where something is, which other forms can copy in.

subtitle: A reusable YANG building block for saying where something is, on Earth, the Moon or any other astronomical body.

tldr.problem: Many network data models need to record where something is, such as a data center, a router or a fiber break, and each model would otherwise invent its own way to do it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9179 defines a YANG grouping called geo-location with a reference frame, either latitude/longitude/height or Cartesian x/y/z coordinates, an optional velocity, and timestamps. It also creates an IANA registry of geodetic system names.
tldr.outcome: Other YANG modules can include the grouping instead of defining their own, and it maps onto common formats such as geo URIs, the W3C geolocation API, GML and KML.

today: RFC 9179 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2022, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. Other YANG modules can use its geo-location grouping, and the geodetic system registry it created is kept by IANA.

sections.title: Why a Shared Location Grouping
sections.content:
Networks often need to say where things are: a data center, a rack at an Internet exchange point, a router, a firewall, a port, the endpoints of a fiber, or the point where a fiber failed. The location need not be on Earth either. The RFC imagines a network on the Moon, on Mars, on Enceladus, or even on a comet, and also locations in simulations or virtual realities.

RFC 9179 defines a single geo-location YANG grouping that can capture all of this. A grouping is a reusable set of definitions that other YANG modules pull in with uses. The specification conforms to ISO 6709:2008, and the module follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) defined in RFC 8342.

Because the module defines only a grouping, it is a building block for the designers of other modules rather than a model that a device implements on its own.
sections.eli5: Instead of every team drawing its own "where is it?" form, everyone shares one good form. It even has room for places that are not on Earth.

sections.title: The Frame of Reference
sections.content:
The reference-frame says what the location values mean. It has three parts.

  • astronomical-body names the body, as defined by the International Astronomical Union, such as a planet, a moon, an asteroid or a comet. The default is earth.
  • geodetic-datum, inside geodetic-system, says what the coordinates mean and where height zero is. The default is wgs-84, the World Geodetic System used by the Global Positioning System (GPS) among many others. Standard values come from an IANA registry.
  • coord-accuracy and height-accuracy can override the accuracy implied by the datum.

There is also an optional feature, alternate-systems, which adds an alternate-system value. Normally it is absent, which means the natural universe is the system. It is meant for things like virtual realities or alternate coordinate systems, and defining such systems is outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: Before you say "it is here", you say which map you are using. Earth, the Moon and a video game each need their own map.

sections.title: Location, Motion and Time
sections.content:
The location itself is a choice of two forms. The ellipsoid form uses latitude and longitude in decimal degrees plus an optional height in meters. The Cartesian form uses x, y and z in meters. In both, the exact meaning comes from the geodetic datum.

For objects in relatively stable motion, a velocity container holds v-north, v-east and v-up, in meters per second. The first two are relative to true north for the body, and v-up points away from the center of mass. Speed and heading can be derived from them: speed is the square root of v-north squared plus v-east squared, and heading is the arctangent of v-east divided by v-north. The velocity can even track very slow movement such as continental drift. More complex motion is out of scope.

Two optional timestamps complete the grouping. timestamp is the time the location was recorded, and valid-until is when it stops being valid; if it is missing, the location has no specific expiry. Where locations nest, such as a building containing routers, a module may say the reference frame is inherited from the container. Attributes such as orientation are deliberately left out because they describe the object, not its location.
sections.eli5: You can say where something is with latitude and longitude, like a map pin, or with three distances from a starting point. If it is moving, you can add which way and how fast.

sections.title: Fit with Other Location Formats
sections.content:
To check that the grouping is portable, the RFC compares it with several existing formats. Where a mapping loses anything, it is mostly a small loss of precision in extreme cases, because the grouping uses decimal64 values.

  • geo URI (RFC 5870): values map to and from the grouping, with the possible precision loss noted above.
  • W3C Geolocation API: fields such as latitude, longitude, altitude, accuracy, heading and speed have counterparts in the grouping.
  • GML: gml:pos values map directly, and mapping the grouping to GML is fully supported for Earth-based geodetic systems. Only the timestamp of gml:Observation is mappable.
  • KML: mapping works in both directions for the ignored-height and absolute-height cases, but not for the relative-to-ground or relative-to-sea-floor cases. For those, the application has to convert to an absolute height first.

The RFC also reports on the ISO 6709:2008 conformance tests. The module always indicates the coordinate reference system or has a default, and it does not define its own coordinate reference system or a text string format, which conformance does not require.
sections.eli5: The form was checked against the other ways people write down places, like web maps and map files. Most things copy across, with only tiny rounding differences.

sections.title: The Geodetic System Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a "Geodetic System Values" registry under "YANG Geographic Location Parameters". It gives one standard name for each geodetic system, even though systems often go by several names. Values SHOULD use an acronym when one exists, MUST be lowercase, and spaces MUST become dashes.

The initial entries are me (Mean Earth/Polar Axis for the Moon), wgs-84-96, wgs-84-08 and wgs-84. The plain wgs-84 entry uses a geoid updated by at least EGM96 for heights, and the other two pin down a more precise definition.

The registration policy is First Come First Served, because the aim is only to avoid duplicates. This differs on purpose from the geo URI crs registry of RFC 5870, which has a very strict modification policy to discourage proliferation. The module also broadens the scope beyond Earth, so an easier registry fits better. The RFC also registers an XML namespace and the ietf-geo-location module name.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of map names so nobody invents two names for the same map. Adding a name to the list is easy, as long as it is not already taken.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed through management protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040), whose secure transports are SSH and TLS. Access can be limited with the NETCONF access control model of RFC 8341.

Since the module defines only groupings, these considerations are mainly for designers of modules that use it. None of the writable data nodes is by itself more sensitive than standard configuration. Some readable nodes may be sensitive in some environments, so read access should be controlled.

Because the grouping identifies locations, authors using it SHOULD consider privacy issues when the data is readable, for example the locations of customer devices.
sections.eli5: Knowing exactly where something is can be private information. So whoever uses this form should decide carefully who gets to read it.
